title: Episode 239: Alexander Hamilton: The Immigrant Bastard, the Treasury, and the Duel at Weehawken
description:
The electrifying life of Alexander Hamilton: the penniless Caribbean orphan who rose to become Washington's right hand, author the Federalist Papers, engineer the American capitalist financial system, and die in the tragic duel against Aaron Burr.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. Today, our chronicle of the Top 50 Famous Non-President Americans follows the fiery, polarizing, and brilliant architect of American capitalism and constitutional governance: Alexander Hamilton.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE HURRICANE CHILD OF THE CARIBBEAN: NEVIS AND ST. CROIX
In January 1755 or 1757, Alexander Hamilton was born out of wedlock on the sun-baked, sugar-rich Caribbean island of Nevis, branded by society with the cruel epithet of an 'illegitimate bastard'. His Scottish merchant father abandoned the family; his mother, Rachel Faucette, died of tropical yellow fever in the same bed where young Alexander lay delirious with sickness. Orphaned at age twelve with no inheritance, Hamilton took a job as an apprentice clerk at the mercantile trading house of Beekman and Cruger on Christiansted, St. Croix. Working long hours over ledgers, calculating exchange rates in Dutch guilders, Spanish pieces of eight, and British pounds, the boy acquired a sophisticated practical mastery of international finance, shipping, and commodities. In August 1772, a ferocious hurricane devastated St. Croix, smashing plantations and hurling ships onto the town streets. The sixteen-year-old Hamilton wrote a vivid, apocalyptic account of the storm in a local newspaper that stunned readers with its literary brilliance and emotional depth. Moved by his genius, wealthy island planters took up a collection to send the teenage prodigy to North America to receive an education, sending him aboard a merchant ship to New York—a penniless immigrant about to reshape the destiny of a continent.  In Christiansted, young Hamilton lived above the counting house on King Street, rising before dawn to inspect cargo manifests of rum, sugar, and enslaved laborers unloaded on the docks.  When Hamilton departed St. Croix, the island's Presbyterian minister Hugh Knox gave him a blessing that proved prophetic: 'Go, young man, and become an ornament to your species.'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: WASHINGTON'S RIGHT HAND: THE CONTINENTAL ARTILLERY AND HEADQUARTERS
Arriving in New York on the eve of the American Revolution, Hamilton threw himself into studies at King's College, today's Columbia University, while publishing brilliant anonymous political pamphlets defending the Boston Tea Party and the Continental Congress. When war erupted, Hamilton raised a provincial New York artillery company, selling his books and clothes to buy uniforms and cannons for his men. At the Battle of Trenton in December 1776, Hamilton's two six-pounder guns fired down King and Queen Streets into the Hessian barracks, covering Washington's surprise crossing of the icy Delaware. Impressed by his cool tactical courage and extraordinary literary mind, General George Washington appointed the twenty-two-year-old captain as his chief aide-de-camp. For four crucial years, Hamilton was Washington's intellectual voice and indispensable right hand, drafting hundreds of official military dispatches, diplomatic letters to Congress, and intelligence communiqués from freezing headquarters at Valley Forge and Morristown, observing firsthand the disastrous paralysis caused by a weak, penniless Confederation government unable to feed or clothe its own army.  At Valley Forge, Hamilton shared a drafty log hut with John Laurens and the Marquis de Lafayette, forging an intimate brotherhood of young revolutionary idealists who shared his vision of an energetic national republic.  In the Revolutionary War, Hamilton's personal letters to his future wife Elizabeth Schuyler, daughter of General Philip Schuyler, revealed a passionate romantic soul behind his cool mathematical intellect.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE ASSAULT ON REDOUBT 10 AT YORKTOWN: OCTOBER 14, 1781
Desperate for battlefield glory to cement his reputation, Hamilton chafed at desk duties and repeatedly petitioned Washington for a field command. In the autumn of 1781, during the Siege of Yorktown in Virginia, Washington granted Hamilton's wish, appointing him to lead the elite American assault battalion against British Redoubt Number 10, while French troops assaulted Redoubt Number 9. On the night of October 14, 1781, Hamilton led four hundred light infantrymen across the muddy trenches under cover of darkness. To ensure maximum surprise, Hamilton ordered his men to unload their muskets and fix their bayonets, forbidding them from firing a single shot that might alert the British sentries. Leaping over the abatis of sharpened tree trunks under heavy musket fire, Hamilton was the first to scramble onto the parapet of the redoubt, urging his men forward with drawn sword. In ten minutes of ferocious hand-to-hand combat in the trenches, Hamilton's battalion overwhelmed the British garrison without losing a single officer. The capture of Redoubts 9 and 10 allowed American siege artillery to bombard the inner British lines at point-blank range, forcing Lord Cornwallis to surrender five days later and winning the Revolutionary War.  Hamilton's bayonet assault on Redoubt Number 10 was executed with such speed and ferocity that the entire British garrison was captured in less than ten minutes with minimal American casualties.  Hamilton's battalion at Yorktown was celebrated for its discipline: despite fighting British soldiers who had committed atrocities in the South, Hamilton prevented his men from harming a single captured British soldier.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE FEDERALIST PAPERS: THE BLUEPRINT OF THE CONSTITUTION
Following the war, Hamilton established a lucrative law practice in New York, helped found the Bank of New York, and became the driving intellectual force behind the movement to replace the bankrupt Articles of Confederation. At the Annapolis Convention of 1786, Hamilton drafted the resolution calling for a Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia. When the new Constitution faced furious Anti-Federalist opposition in New York, Hamilton conceived the most celebrated series of political essays in world history: The Federalist Papers. Writing under the Roman pseudonym 'Publius', Hamilton enlisted James Madison and John Jay to produce an astonishing torrent of eighty-five essays in just six months, composed aboard Hudson River packet boats and in late-night law offices. While Jay wrote five and Madison twenty-nine, Hamilton authored fifty-one masterworks of political philosophy, systematically defending an energetic executive branch, a strong national defense, a sovereign federal taxation power, and an independent judicial branch possessing the power of judicial review. The Federalist Papers remain the definitive intellectual commentary on the United States Constitution, celebrated globally as a masterpiece of republican political theory.  In Federalist Number 78, Hamilton formulated the definitive American doctrine of judicial review, explaining that the Constitution is the supreme fundamental law and that courts must declare unconstitutional any legislative act that violates it.  In Federalist Number 70, Hamilton famously argued that 'energy in the executive is a leading character in the definition of good government,' warning that a feeble executive leads to a feeble execution of the laws.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE FIRST SECRETARY OF THE TREASURY: INVENTING AMERICAN CAPITALISM
In September 1789, President George Washington appointed thirty-two-year-old Hamilton as the first Secretary of the Treasury. The nation's finances were in absolute ruin: the federal government owed seventy-nine million dollars in war debts, paper continental currency was worthless, and international credit was non-existent. In a series of brilliant landmark reports submitted to Congress—the Report on Public Credit, the Report on a National Bank, and the Report on Manufactures—Hamilton engineered the modern American capitalist financial system. He boldly proposed the 'assumption' of all state debts by the federal government, converting chaotic obligations into unified federal bonds, famously declaring that 'a national debt, if it is not excessive, will be to us a national blessing' by binding the interests of wealthy creditors to the survival of the union. He created the Bank of the United States, established the United States Mint, founded the Revenue Marine—precursor to the Coast Guard—and advocated for tariffs to protect infant American manufacturing. Thomas Jefferson and James Madison vehemently opposed Hamilton's vision, fearing an urban financial aristocracy, but in the famous 'Dinner Deal' of 1790, Jefferson agreed to Hamilton's financial program in exchange for moving the permanent national capital to the banks of the Potomac River.  Hamilton's creation of the Revenue Marine in 1790 deployed armed cutters to patrol coastal waters, enforcing customs collections and interdicting smugglers to guarantee the flow of federal tariff revenue.  Hamilton's vision of an industrial, commercial America dominated by cities, factories, and banks directly triumphed over Jefferson's agrarian vision, laying the economic foundation for the modern superpower.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE REYNOLDS AFFAIR: THE FIRST GREAT POLITICAL SEX SCANDAL
Hamilton's soaring political career met a devastating self-inflicted catastrophe in the summer of 1797. Five years earlier, while serving as Treasury Secretary, Hamilton had engaged in an illicit extramarital affair in Philadelphia with a twenty-three-year-old married woman named Maria Reynolds. When her corrupt husband, James Reynolds, discovered the liaison, he blackmailed Hamilton, extorting hundreds of dollars in hush money. When political enemies accused Hamilton of financial speculation with public treasury funds, Hamilton chose to protect his financial honor by committing political suicide: he published a sensational, ninety-five-page tell-all pamphlet entitled Observations on Certain Documents, known as the Reynolds Pamphlet. In excruciating detail, Hamilton confessed to the adulterous affair, printing Maria's intimate love letters to prove that he had not misappropriated a single penny of public money. While his financial integrity was vindicated, his personal reputation was shattered; his wife Elizabeth Schuyler was devastated, and his hopes of ever attaining the presidency were buried forever under a mountain of public scandal and ridicule.  When the Reynolds Pamphlet was published, Hamilton's political allies were stunned by his raw candor, but his uncompromising honesty demonstrated that he placed personal honor above political self-preservation.  Hamilton's wife Elizabeth Schuyler Hamilton forgave her husband for the Reynolds affair, standing by him through the political firestorm with unwavering dignity and devotion.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE DUEL AT WEEHAWKEN: JULY 11, 1804
The bitter political rivalry between Hamilton and Vice President Aaron Burr reached a fatal climax during the New York gubernatorial election of 1804. After Burr was defeated, he learned that Hamilton had made disparaging remarks at an Albany dinner party, allegedly calling Burr 'a dangerous man who ought not to be trusted with the reins of government'. When Hamilton refused to issue a categorical apology, Burr challenged him to a duel with pistols under the code duello. On the humid morning of July 11, 1804, the two men crossed the Hudson River by rowing boat to a narrow, secluded ledge beneath the high palisades of Weehawken, New Jersey—the very spot where Hamilton's nineteen-year-old eldest son, Philip, had been killed in a duel three years earlier. Prior to the encounter, Hamilton wrote in a private letter that his Christian conscience compelled him to 'fire his pistol into the air' to avoid shedding blood. Standing ten paces apart, the word was given: Hamilton raised his hair-trigger Wogdon pistol and fired high into the branches of a cedar tree above Burr's head. Burr aimed with deadly precision: his lead ball tore through Hamilton's abdomen, shattering a rib and lodging in his spine. Hamilton collapsed into the arms of his physician, murmuring: 'This is a mortal wound, Doctor.' Transported back to Manhattan, Hamilton died thirty hours later at age forty-nine, leaving his faithful wife Eliza to spend the next fifty years preserving the memory and monumental legacy of the immigrant orphan who built the financial foundation of the American empire.  Following the fatal shot at Weehawken, Hamilton's second Nathaniel Pendleton and Burr's second William Van Ness kept the duel secret until the mortally wounded statesman could be carried across the Hudson to Manhattan.  Aaron Burr lived the remainder of his life shadowed by Hamilton's death, later attempting to carve out an empire in the West and dying in obscurity on Staten Island in 1836.

[Rebecca - Host]
